title: 🚨 I’ve been following Gil Durán for several years, initially through the @FramelabNews @X account, and I highly recommend engaging with his essential investigative journalism and political commentary.
content:
🚨 I’ve been following Gil Durán for several years, initially through the @FramelabNews @X account, and I highly recommend engaging with his essential investigative journalism and political commentary.

His own X account was permanently suspended around April 20–21, 2026. His suspension appeal was denied.

I strongly recommend everyone buy and read his new meticulously researched book, which he's been working on and revising for years, ‘The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy’, which is finally being is published on 18 August (Simon & Schuster, £25).

I reprint today’s Guardian article about him ‘If we don’t fight back, we don’t have a future’: the journalist taking on the ‘tech fascists’ of Silicon Valley, in full (link below):

As Elon Musk, Peter Thiel and their peers have grown richer and more influential, Gil Durán argues they have all but abandoned democracy – and found the perfect government to enable them.

In April, Gil Durán was permanently banned from Elon Musk’s X for posting just two words.

Durán was responding to a post from the tech company #Palantir outlining its 22‑point “technological manifesto”,  which praised American “hard power”, western culture and AI weapons, denounced inclusivity and called for compulsory national service.

Durán  responded: “TLDR: Fascism” (TLDR is short for “too long, didn’t read”).

Durán didn’t break any of X’s written rules, he points out over a video call from San Francisco – so much for Musk’s “free-speech absolutism”. 

His ban might just have had something to do with his preceding tweet, showing the cover of his new book, The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy.

The book’s central argument is that big tech is no longer our friend, as many of its billionaire owners have seized economic and political control and are steering the fate of the planet towards their own bizarre, apocalyptic visions.

Fascism is no exaggeration, Durán asserts. He researched multiple definitions – by Umberto Eco, Robert Paxton, Jason Stanley – and decided that Donald Trump’s Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement ticks all the boxes.

“It’s a cult of grievance that seeks to purge its enemies by demonising them through absurd and surreal  propaganda that exploits fears over law and order and gender and sexuality in order to seize power and install a permanent hierarchy that fascists consider the moral order of the world and the universe. In addition, you also have this sort of nationalistic, militaristic vibe.”

By extension, he says, Silicon Valley is fascist “because they have wholly aligned with a fascist movement.  That’s their vehicle for gaining power.”

Few could dispute this alignment after seeing the bosses of Meta, Google, Apple, Amazon and  OpenAI line up behind Trump at his second inauguration, or Musk’s now shuttered “department of government efficiency” (DOGE) being given free rein to conduct mass firings of federal employees, or Palantir’s AI-driven surveillance technology enabling deportations by Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

It’s a cosy relationship, Durán says: the tech titans have helped Trump and his family become billionaires through cryptocurrency and have been given government contracts and freedom from regulation or oversight.

In addition, Durán believes, “Silicon Valley has gone fascist because they have adopted an extreme ideology of tech supremacy.” While Maga promises a return to a mythical glorious past, he says, the “technofascists” are promising a mythical glorious future: “We’re going to be in the stars. We’re going to be in space. And all we need is to  get rid of anybody who stands in our way as we seek to accelerate technology toward this speedy, violent, God-like transcendence that we will achieve if we can only burn enough energy and enough compute to bring our boom loop into existence.”

It sounds almost like a conspiracy theory, but Durán is not short of evidence.

Musk making an apparent Nazi salute and describing empathy as “the fundamental weakness of western civilisation”.

Palantir’s Peter Thiel [who Nigel Farage refers to as his “friend”] writing in 2009 that “I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible” and giving a lecture series suggesting Greta Thunberg could be the antichrist.

Marc Andreessen, the CEO of the tech investment company Andreessen Horowitz, paraphrasing Filippo Tommaso Marinetti, the co-author of  Mussolini’s Fascist Manifesto, in his “Techno-Optimist Manifesto”: “Technology must be a violent assault on the forces of the unknown, to force them to bow before man.”

Durán, a journalist and former political adviser, lays out the narrative in exacting detail, outlining the connections between these men (and it is all men) and the origins of their often deeply weird beliefs, many  of which view everyone outside their circle or opposed to their agenda as expendable.

Unpacking all their overlapping  philosophies would take some time, but TLDR: “It’s the idea that what matters more is the billions or trillions of people yet unborn in the future. And the only way they’re going to get to be born is if this elite group of white tech figures and gazillionaires makes the right decisions to make the human race transhuman and multiplanetary through AI and technology,” says Durán. “By becoming a billionaire, they all  have this idea that they’re superior to everyone else. They are susceptible to this kind of thinking.”

Durán, 50, is almost the opposite: the son of working-class Mexican immigrants in California. He was the first in his family to go to college, having grown up in relative poverty: “It made me tough and gave me an unyielding loyalty to regular people over the many rich and powerful people I’ve spent a lot of my time around.”

Durán’s  book traces the roots of this movement to two important sources. One is the 1997 book The Sovereign Individual, written by the American  investor James Dale Davidson and William Rees-Mogg, the former Times  editor and BBC grandee (and father of Jacob).

Their book prophesied how digital tools such as the internet and cryptocurrency would pave the way for a privatised, corporatised, unregulated, post-democratic future ruled by rich, powerful, unaccountable individuals.

Two decades later, this led to the idea of “network states” – digital realms beyond the jurisdiction of nation  states – as popularised by Balaji Srinivasan, a former partner at Andreessen Horowitz.

The other source is Curtis Yarvin, a former software developer and armchair philosopher with a penchant for psychedelics, sometimes referred to as the godfather of the “dark enlightenment”.

In pseudonymous blogs in the late 2000s, Yarvin outlined a worldview in which liberal democracy had failed to deliver progress, partly because institutions such as education and the media had been captured by what  he called “the Cathedral”.

His proposed solution was a mass firing of government employees (he coined the acronym “Rage”, “retire all government employees”) and the installation of a “national CEO, [or] what’s called a dictator”.

Yarvin also mused about a “humane alternative to genocide” to deal with unproductive citizens and has had to deny accusations that he is a white supremacist  or supports racist ideologies.

Scratch the surface, Durán suggests, and Yarvin’s ideas have much in common with Nazi ideologies, “but updated as  rightwing dogma for the blogging age”.

Both of these sources might have languished in obscurity had it not been for Thiel, the man at the heart of Silicon Valley’s rightward lurch. He has amassed enormous wealth through a series of investments in tech  startups – first PayPal, then Facebook, Spotify, LinkedIn, Palantir and OpenAI, among others.

He was the first major tech figure to back Donald Trump, in July 2016, and persuaded others to follow, including Andreessen, who said he spent half his time at Mar-a-Lago in the month after Trump won the 2024 election.

Thiel liked The Sovereign Individual so much that he wrote a new introduction when it was reprinted in 2020. He has also made steps to found his own  network state – first via the ill-fated “seasteading” movement (establishing floating countries in international waters) then via Próspera, a “special economic zone” on an island in Honduras. 

Incorporated in 2017 with permission from the Honduran government and  reportedly co-funded by Srinivasan, Andreessen and OpenAI’s Sam Altman,  Próspera has sought to attract digital startups with loose regulations (appealing to longevity researchers), low taxes and a crypto-friendly economy.

Other similar projects have sprung up. In 2021, the president of El Salvador, Nayib Bukele, hailed the mooted creation of a “Bitcoin City”.  In 2023, Trump announced plans to build 10 “Freedom Cities” on  government land across the US, with input from Próspera representatives. In 2024, Srinivasan founded a “Network School” in Johor, Malaysia.

Thiel also began to absorb Yarvin’s theories about how the political order was preventing progress. In the 2009 essay in which Thiel declared the incompatibility of freedom and democracy, he also said “the vast increase in welfare beneficiaries and the extension of the franchise to women” made capitalist democracy  impossible, which did not win him many mainstream supporters.

But Yarvin backed up Thiel and the two became friends and allies. “While The Sovereign Individual provided the foundation for the billionaire’s political vision, Yarvin created a blueprint for turning that vision into reality,” Durán writes.

Thiel was instrumental in injecting these ideas, and people, into the US  government – not least JD Vance, whom Durán describes as “almost  entirely a creation of Peter Thiel”.

It was Thiel who set up Vance as a venture capitalist, giving him a role at his firm Mithril Capital, then  investing in Vance’s own fund, Narya Capital (Tolkien-derived names are a  theme with these people).

It was Thiel who backed Vance’s move into politics, where he went from condemning Trump as “America’s Hitler” to supporting him and parroting Yarvin’s ideas. “I think that what Trump should do, if I was giving him one piece of advice: fire every single mid-level bureaucrat, every civil servant in the administrative state, replace them with our people,” Vance told the podcaster Jack Murphy in 2021.

Durán had observed this Silicon Valley takeover developing and began writing about it in 2024. “I thought this would be a problem in five to 10  years, but when JD Vance got on the ticket, it suddenly took on a new  urgency,” he says.

Now, it almost feels too late.

In 2025, Bloomberg reported that at least 16 men connected to Thiel and his companies occupied  positions of power in the Trump administration, including David Sacks, who is now a special adviser for AI and crypto. Musk’s Doge has swung  its chainsaw at the government, crypto and AI regulation has all but  disappeared, the Trump family are now billionaires, and the tech oligarchs have become the Republicans’ largest donors.

At the same time, they have become substantial beneficiaries of the very government they once sought to dismantle. Palantir has an estimated $13.7 BILLION in US government contracts; last year, its stock price rose more than 90% in six months. Andreessen is backing dozens of defence companies scooping up government contracts and recently joined the Pentagon’s advisory board. Last week, Musk’s SpaceX received a $1.6 BILLION contract to supply rockets to the US Space Force – on the same day he pledged at least $100 MILLION to help Republicans in November’s midterm elections.

“It’s a severe cautionary tale about the hazards of privatisation,” says Durán. “The government created these men, especially Elon Musk. And now these welfare kings want to pull up the ladder, want to destroy  the very system that made them. This is a massive failure by the US intelligence apparatus – to not see this threat forming from the inside.”

Durán, who worked in communications  for Kamala Harris when she was California’s attorney general, as well as for the late Democratic senator Dianne Feinstein, blames the Democrats as much as the Republicans: “They have failed tremendously to stand up to billionaire power because the only people as  addicted to billionaire money in American politics as the Republicans are the Democrats,” he says.

He singles out the California governor, Gavin Newsom,  as a prime example of a “Silicon Valley Democrat”: “You don’t see him criticising these guys. He only goes after Trump, Trump, Trump and  Vance, Vance, Vance … You want some viral content? Why don’t you go off on Peter Thiel’s weird antichrist obsession?”

Even if the Democrats take control after the midterms or the 2028 presidential election, Durán is worried that “these tech fascists will win… because Democrats will not hold them accountable”.

On  the plus side, the Silicon Valley takeover has not been going that well  lately. Network states around the world are losing ground. In 2021,  Próspera’s special economic status was repealed by the new president,  Xiomara Castro (it is suing the Honduran government for $10.8 BILLION). Two weeks ago, Srinivasan’s Network School was ordered to close (Srinivasan says he is moving it to Kazakhstan). Trump’s Freedom Cities remain unbuilt.

One saving grace, says Durán, is that “a lot of these people don’t really have a great grasp of on-the-ground  realities”. Nobody really wants to live in a soulless network state, he says: “Why would you be in Kazakhstan instead of San Francisco, which is the global capital of tech?” On the other hand, he points out, the tech billionaires have effectively turned the US into a de facto network state.

But they may well have overplayed their hand. “Silicon Valley oligarchs are really vulnerable right now,” says Durán. “People don’t like them. People are starting to rise up against data centres and this vision of an AI apocalypse that kills all the jobs and potentially kills all of humanity. You’re scaring the hell out of people and now they don’t like you. Into that could step a politician to take advantage of that trend and come up with a message that speaks to the concerns of people and against the dark fantasies of the oligarchs.”

The question now, he says, “is how we turn the momentum in our favour and against the billionaires. Because they have a plan to win. They think they’re going to succeed.”

This could be a radicalising moment: “In fighting against billionaire power, we find the key to all of our problems. Every moment is an important opportunity to wake people up and to start to fight back.”

If not, he says, we’ll find ourselves in a situation where “we don’t have democracy, we don’t have an economy, and we don’t have a future. If that doesn’t radicalise people, then we deserve what we’re going to get.”

--ENDS--

Please read, share, and act - before it’s too late. 🙏

title:
Jane Street pays 22-year-olds $700k to fail one coin-flip game the right way. I found out why the hard way, when my own bet-sizing model told me to put the whole account on a single trade.

I watched
content:
Jane Street pays 22-year-olds $700k to fail one coin-flip game the right way. I found out why the hard way, when my own bet-sizing model told me to put the whole account on a single trade.

I watched Dwarkesh tour their Texas data center this week. $6 billion of CoreWeave compute, racks of GPUs under liquid cooling, a firm scaling toward hundreds of thousands of chips. The point the whole tour builds to is not the hardware. It is that they still hire humans, because the models break at what they call phase transitions, the moments the market moves most and the training data stops describing the world.

So they screen for the one thing a model cannot fake: do you hold when the math and your gut point in opposite directions. The test they use is a coin flip written down in 1738.

I built my sizer to maximize expected value. Feed it an edge, it hands back a size. On my highest-conviction signal it wanted 100 percent of the book. The first "sure" edge that broke the other way took the account with it. I went hunting for the bug in my code. The bug was three centuries old.

The game is the St. Petersburg paradox. A pot starts at $2 and doubles on every flip. You win the pot the moment the first heads lands. Heads on flip k pays 2^k, with probability 1/2^k.

Expected value:

sum (1/2^k)(2^k) = 1 + 1 + 1 + ... = infinity

The math says the ticket is worth infinite money. Nobody sane pays $20 for it. That split, between what the number says and what you would actually do, is the whole test. Here your gut is right.

Daniel Bernoulli published the fix in St. Petersburg in 1738. Stop maximizing money. Maximize its utility, where each extra dollar is worth less than the last one:

maximize E[ln(wealth)], not E[wealth]

Take the log and infinity collapses to a finite number. Risk aversion falls straight out of the arithmetic.

This is Kelly. John Kelly rederived Bernoulli in 1956 to size bets:

f* = (bp - q) / b

f* is the fraction of the account to risk, b the net odds, p the win probability, q the rest. Maximizing log wealth caps every bet, including the one my EV model wanted to shove everything into.

All that compute, and the edge they protect is a human who does not break at the phase transition. Bernoulli has been dead 244 years. The fix sat free in a library the whole time. I paid for it in drawdown first.

- it's cool and high status

- it's more entertaining to say it that way
- losers are louder than winners, so you get unrepresentative samples
- something that works now might have side effects that you don't see until later
- something that works in one population, place, time, institution doesn't work in another
- it seems true when a prestigious person or institution puts their approval on it
- old claims stick around because systems, habits, or contracts were built around them and it's too expensive to change
- staying vague lets them have plausible deniability, so the audience can be influenced but the speaker doesn't get blamed
- people make noise so it's harder to identify the actual truth
- there's too many things to check so people get lazy and just believe what is convenient
- it's easier to believe something that fits with what you already know than what could falsify a lot of your beliefs
- if it sounds right, it seems right
- if it sounds new, it seems better than what's old
- believing the opposite makes you look intelligent or independent because they don't want to be a "sheep"
- mistakes multiply because of bad reviews, replication, bias, moderation
- it's safe to say it. nobody gets fired for repeating the consensus
- they're too dumb to imagine a path that worked for them under a narrow set of circumstances, and apply it as a law
- people are mentally ill and say things to get it out of their system, not because it's true

protect your brain's training data. stop believing everything you see online.

here's how I use my own brain:

all advice should be modeled like an engineering problem. find the inputs, outputs, constraints

think of this sentence: “when I drop this pen, it falls to the ground”

sounds obvious, but here's how I look at it:

input: I’m on Earth, I’m holding a pen, I let go of it, and nothing else is exerting enough force to keep it suspended

output: the pen accelerates downwards and eventually hits the ground

failure modes: someone catches it. it lands on a table. a strong upward force keeps it from falling. I’m underwater. I’m in orbit. there’s no meaningful gravity. the pen is tied to a string and I’ve somehow failed to notice

“when I drop this pen, it falls to the ground” is conditionally true. ALL advice works like this.

what this means is that every belief has operating conditions. every claim works inside a particular environment, under a particular set of assumptions, until one of those assumptions stops being true.

the problem is that the conditions are removed because it's a better clickbait headline.

so before taking any advice, ask:
- what are the inputs?
- what is the output?
- how could it fail?
- who benefits from my believing it?
- and, what happens in the long-run if I believe this?

because it doesn’t take a mastermind to come up with slop that ends up rotting your brain.

content:
This video is fake. The labor monopoly it previews isn’t.

A CGI robot dances behind a kitchen counter in a cowboy hat. Another takes over the living room while a human reaches past them for a drink.

It looks like a futuristic house party. But the real story is not robots entertaining people at home.

It is robots learning to operate inside human spaces before humans send them somewhere with no roads, no oxygen, and no Wi-Fi.

The second robot moves through a normal apartment built for human bodies: doors, counters, mirrors, furniture. That is exactly why Tesla keeps betting on legs, hands, and local intelligence instead of cheaper warehouse carts.

Wheels dominate flat factory floors. Legs matter when the floor disappears.

Earth gives Optimus kitchens, warehouses, factories, and millions of hours of training data. Mars gives Tesla the market nobody else can reach.

One human on Mars needs life support, training, protection, and a return plan.

One robot needs power and a one-way ticket.
The dancing robot is CGI.
The business model is not.

Wall Street sees a machine learning to move through a living room.

Musk sees the first workforce waiting at the bottom of a Starship.

title:
Better AI models aren't enough to build better robots.

They need better data.

That's exactly what @axisrobotics is solving with Axis Dataset V1, a community-driven robotics dataset built on @base.
content:
Better AI models aren't enough to build better robots.

They need better data.

That's exactly what @axisrobotics is solving with Axis Dataset V1, a community-driven robotics dataset built on @base.

The first release includes:

• 207 tabletop manipulation tasks 
• 50,000+ human demonstrations 
• 60,000+ task and scene variants 
• 7 real-world environments, from kitchens to offices

The impressive part isn't just the scale.

Anyone can contribute through a browser by controlling simulated robots. No expensive hardware, no robotics lab, and no local GPU required.

The results speak for themselves.

Training with the full Axis dataset increased LIBERO-Plus benchmark performance from 83.9% to 88.8%, with the biggest improvements in robustness against camera changes, sensor noise, and robot pose variations.

Even more interesting, a volume-matched control dataset performed far worse, showing that data quality and diversity matter more than simply collecting more trajectories.

This is a glimpse of how Physical AI could scale: thousands of contributors generating high-quality training data together, with transparent onchain provenance.

The future of robotics won't just be built in labs.

It'll be built by communities on @base. 💙

author: masamune_sakaki

title:
医学教育へのAI利用
 
AIを医学教育から排除するのではなく、AIを使うことを前提に、研修医の臨床推論をどう守り、どう伸ばすか。

Abdulnour RE, et al. Educational Strategies for Clinical Supervision of Artificial Intelligence Use. N Engl J Med. 2025;393:786-797.
content:
医学教育へのAI利用
 
AIを医学教育から排除するのではなく、AIを使うことを前提に、研修医の臨床推論をどう守り、どう伸ばすか。

Abdulnour RE, et al. Educational Strategies for Clinical Supervision of Artificial Intelligence Use. N Engl J Med. 2025;393:786-797. 

重要ポイント
1．この論文の核心
臨床推論そのものをAIに丸投げすると、独力で考える能力が育たない危険がある。AIに「考えてもらう」のではなく、AIを使いながら「自分で考える」能力を育てることが医学教育の目標になる。

その中心となる能力がadaptive practice（適応的実践）とcritical thinking（批判的思考）である。すなわち、慣れた問題では効率よく対応し、未知・不確実な問題では立ち止まって柔軟に考える能力だ。

2．AI時代に最も怖い「3つの-skilling」
AIを適切に使えば学習曲線を押し上げられる一方、学習早期からの無批判な依存はnever-skilling（本来身につけるべき能力を最初から獲得しない）、deskilling（すでに獲得した能力が低下）、mis-skilling（AIの誤りやバイアスを学習してしまう）につながる。

3．「AIを使えば診断能力が上がる」とは限らない
大規模言語モデル（LLM）は知識問題だけでなく、複雑な診断、診断推論、management reasoning（病名を確定後、どのような治療や検査、経過観察を行うかを決定する思考プロセス）などでも高い性能を示す。

しかし、LLMには作話やバイアスがあるため最終的な診断・治療判断は人間が担うべきである。

さらに興味深いのは、「医師＋AI」が必ずしも「AI単独」より優れているわけではないという点である。AIが医師より優秀な状況では、人間がAIをうまく利用できず、組み合わせることでかえって成績が悪化することがある。

一方、もともとの臨床能力が高い医師では、人間＋AIによってperformanceが改善する。

4．最重要：DEFT-AI
指導医が研修医のAI使用を見つけたとき、その瞬間は臨床推論を教える絶好の機会となる。

D：Diagnosis / Discussion / Discourse
まず研修医自身の思考過程を確認する。
「この患者のプロブレムをどうプレゼンした？」、「AIを使う前の鑑別は？」、「どのAIを使った？」、「どんなプロンプトを入れた？」、「AIの回答で自分の鑑別はどう変わった？」

E：Evidence
次に、「そのAIの回答をどう検証した？」、「支持する所見は？」、「反証する所見は？」、「ガイドラインや論文と一致している？」と尋ねる。

F：Feedback
研修医自身に、「今回のAIの使い方で何がよかった？」、「改善するとしたら？」と自己評価させる。

T：Teaching
そのうえで指導医が、臨床推論、EBM（evidence-based medicine）、AIリテラシー、プロンプトの入力法、AIのバイアスや限界 について必要な部分だけ教える。 

最後に、「この仕事ではAIをどう使うべきか」を具体的に指示する。

5．CentaurとCyborg
Centaur型（ケンタウル型）
人間とAIで仕事を分担する。AIに仕事を任せても、重要な判断は人間が行い、AIのoutputを慎重に検証する。

high-risk／診断／不確実性が高い／AIが十分検証されていない仕事に向く。 
たとえば、「この患者は肺塞栓症でしょうか？」を汎用LLMに相談する場合。AIは鑑別や見落としチェックに使っても、最終判断は医師。
 
Cyborg型（サイボーグ型）
人間とAIが一体となって仕事を進める。AIに案を出させる→修正→再プロンプト→さらに修正という共同作業。

これは、low-risk／well-defined／creative／AIの性能が十分確認されている仕事に向く。 

たとえば、患者説明文の下書き、メール作成、アイデア出し、学習計画作成など。

6．「CentaurかCyborgか」は固定しない（重要）
AIを使う／使わない、ではなく、仕事のリスクに応じてAIとの距離を変える。

診断や重大な治療判断ならCentaur寄り。
文章の下書きやbrainstormingならCyborg寄り。

この切り替える能力そのものがadaptive practice（適応型演習）である。

Adaptive practiceでは、AIを使い一人ひとりの理解度や苦手な部分に合わせて、問題の難易度や出題内容を自動で変えることができる。
 
7．AIの回答は「正しいか」ではなく「検証できるか」
AIが出した回答を自分の臨床判断＋ガイドライン＋文献＋専門家の意見と比較する。

AIと自分の判断が一致すれば信頼度は上がるが、一致しても常に警戒心や注意を持ち続ける必要がある。

8．プロンプト作成も臨床能力の一部になる
「この患者の診断は？」というプロンプトより、患者背景、状況、自分の役割、AIに求めるtaskを具体的に示す。

また、「私は喘息だと思います。診断は？」のような誘導的な指示は、LLMのsycophancy（迎合）を引き起こし、バイアスを強める可能性がある。

title: The Patent Enforcement Economy Is Leaving Inventors Behind/ IPWatchdog Unleashed
content: The patent system makes a promise that has become increasingly conditional. An inventor discloses an invention to the public and, in return, receives a limited right to exclude. On paper, that bargain remains intact. In the real world, however, a patent owner often discovers that functionally the right is only defensible if the infringement is large enough (but not too large), the damages are high enough (but not too high), the portfolio is deep enough, and somebody is willing to finance years of litigation. Our conversation this week for IPWatchdog Unleashed is about what happens after a patent owner has completed the tedious work of understanding what is actually owned and is now ready to pursue a licensing or enforcement campaign. The post The Patent Enforcement Economy Is Leaving Inventors Behind/ <i>IPWatchdog Unleashed</i> appeared first on IPWatchdog.com | Patents & Intellectual Property Law .

title: Ninth Circuit Again Reverses Jack Daniel’s Trademark Win Due to Bad Spaniels’ Successful Parody
content: On Tuesday, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit issued a published ruling reversing the U.S. District Court for the District of Arizona’s entry of permanent injunction for distiller Jack Daniel’s in the long-running trademark case involving VIP Products’ Bad Spaniels dog toy. This latest chapter in the decade-plus-long case remands the decision back to the district court with orders to enter judgment in favor of defendant VIP Products after finding that Jack Daniel’s did not meet its burden to show dilution by tarnishment. title: Federal Circuit Affirms Non-Infringement Ruling in Lidocaine Patch Patent Dispute Over ZTlido Generic
content: The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit (CAFC) issued a decision Tuesday affirming a judgment of non-infringement entered by the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida in a dispute concerning generic versions of the topical pain patch ZTlido. The panel of Judges Reyna, Mayer, and Hughes, ruling per curiam, upheld the district court’s construction of the term “dissolving agent” and its determination that Aveva Drug Delivery Systems’ proposed generic product did not infringe under the doctrine of equivalents. title: After 6,000 Romantasy Pages, Judge Hands Crave Plaintiff the Bill
content: The Crave copyright case was open and shut once a judge compared the books. Getting to the “shut” part took four years and $3.4 million in legal fees. In her March opinion dismissing Lynne Freeman’s copyright infringement lawsuit over Tracy Wolff’s Crave series, Judge Colleen McMahon paused amid 157 pages of legal analysis to inventory the damage: six unpublished drafts, nine sets of notes, and four novels whose print shrank and margins tightened with each successive volume, leaving the court with “upwards of 6,000 pages of romantasy fiction.” “That was a lot of reading,” McMahon observed—the weary understatement of the only person who’d actually finished the assignment for an involuntary book club that doesn’t even serve wine. Her conclusion, after all that reading, was no substantial similarity as a matter of law. The overlaps Freeman cited were the stock ingredients of YA romantasy: a teenage heroine discovering supernatural powers in Alaska, a dangerous love interest, demonic forces, and the usual assortment of cursed bloodlines. As McMahon put it, “hot, sexy, dangerous boys—central to virtually all young adult romance novels—cannot be copyrighted.” Freeman’s fragmented literal similarity theory didn’t fare any better. It relied on Wolff’s use of phrases like “everything is going to be okay,” “tears streaming down my cheeks,” and “well, well, well.” Treating such language as evidence of infringement, McMahon wrote, “trivializes copyright law”—not to mention depriving fictional villains of their go-to line whenever they catch heroes snooping around. “The Court has personally read every word of the four Wolff books and the six Freeman drafts and nine sets of notes at issue in this case. title: Amnesty International demands China release activist arrested for Dalai Lama photo
content: Amnesty International on Wednesday urged Chinese authorities to immediately release a human rights activist who was detained for showing a photograph of the Dalai Lama in a monastery in Tibet, emphasizing that his detention violates fundamental rights to freedom of expression and religion. Zhang Yi, a prominent pro-democracy activist, was arrested on 28 July for “inciting separatism” contrary to China’s new Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress , which came into effect on the 1st of July. The law states its aim as promoting “a strong sense of community” among Chinese people. Article 2 of the law highlights that this must be achieved by “upholding” the Chinese Communist Party’s leadership. Other articles aim to establish homogeny in respect of culture, religion, language/written script, and history, with critics arguing that the legislation serves a sweeping legal tool to enforce forced assimilation and eliminate the distinct cultural identities of minority populations. Notably, Article 63 establishes that the law extends beyond China’s borders; it states that those outside of mainland territory that commit acts contrary to the law or create “ethnic division” are to be pursued in accordance with the law. Rights groups have criticized the government for using a vaguely worded legislation to exercise extraterritorial jurisdiction over diaspora communities, forcing them to live in fear of retaliation from the Chinese government. Zhang Yi was initially detained on 1 July during a visit to a monastery in Tibet. He had showed a Tibetan worshipper a photograph of the Dalai Lama on his phone, in an attempt to non-verbally communicate that he needed a prayer mat, before being arrested by the police. title: Federal workers file class action lawsuit over transgender health coverage ban
content: Five federal workers filed a proposed class-action lawsuit Monday against the Trump administration, alleging that a federal health insurance policy excluding gender-affirming care violates federal employment discrimination law. The complaint , filed in the US District Court for the District of Columbia, challenges an Office of Personnel Management (OPM) directive. The directive requires carriers in federal and postal employee health programs to exclude certain procedures when used for gender transition. OPM issued the directive in August 2025, and the exclusion took effect on the 1st of January 2026. The plaintiffs claim the policy violates Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 , which prohibits sex discrimination in federal employment. They argue that insurers may cover hormone therapy, hysterectomies, and facial surgeries for other medical purposes. However, insurers may deny the same procedures when they are used as gender-affirming care . “This exclusion targets gender-affirming care and thereby singles out current and former employees who are transgender or gender non-conforming,” the complaint states. The five anonymous plaintiffs include employees seeking care for themselves and employees seeking coverage for transgender family members. According to the complaint, some have paid hundreds or thousands of dollars out of pocket. Others have considered using their savings, delayed procedures, or faced the possibility of discontinuing ongoing treatment because of the exclusion. A July report from the Williams Institute, a UCLA School of Law research center, estimated that between 39,400 and 57,800 transgender people receive federal employee health coverage. The plaintiffs seek to represent federal and postal employees denied coverage for their own or a dependent’s gender-affirming care. title: Romania dispatch: government avoids international credit rating downgrade
content: Mihai Coca-Constantinescu, who holds an International and European Law LLB from the University of Groningen and an International Trade and Investment Law LLM from the University of Amsterdam, is a PhD candidate in Transboundary Legal Studies at the University of Groningen, based in the Netherlands, where he covers legal developments in Romania as a JURIST correspondent. On July 31, international credit rating agency Fitch Ratings reaffirmed Romania’s BBB- credit rating, keeping the country at the lowest level considered safe for international investment. The decision spared Romania from a downgrade to “junk” status—a label that signals greater financial risk and can make it more expensive for the government to borrow money. Maintaining its current rating helps preserve investor confidence, avoids the higher borrowing costs that often follow a downgrade, and prevents it from falling into non-investment territory. Fitch cited Romania’s membership in the European Union and continued access to European funding as important sources of economic stability. In particular, the agency pointed to the EU’s National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR), which provides billions of euros in grants and low-interest loans to support reforms, infrastructure, and economic modernization. These European funds help strengthen Romania’s long-term growth prospects and support its ability to manage public debt. However, Fitch maintained a Negative Outlook because of ongoing domestic challenges, including a projected 2026 budget deficit of 5.9% of GDP, inflation expected to remain near 7.6%, and heightened political uncertainty following the collapse of the four-party governing coalition earlier this year. Following the announcement, Romanian President Nicușor Dan addressed the nation on Saturday, August 1, 2026. title: Rights group urges Thailand authorities to protect MPs and rights defender facing online death threats
content: Human Rights Watch on Friday called on authorities in Thailand to take urgent measures to address a wave of online death threats and harassment against members of parliament Angkhana Neelaphaijit and Romadon Panjor, as well as human rights activist Anchana Heemmina, after they voiced their disapproval of actions of the Thai military and expressed their support for the Muslim community in the country’s Deep South. Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch, stated: “The Thai authorities should urgently and impartially investigate online attacks, including death threats, against Angkhana, Anchana, and Romadon, who have been widely recognized for their work defending human rights in Thailand’s deep south… Those responsible for serious threats should be brought to justice, regardless of their affiliation, to demonstrate Thailand’s commitment to protecting human rights defenders.” The HRW statement came as Angkhana filed a police complaint under the Computer-Related Crime Act (CCA) after an online disinformation campaign called for her extrajudicial killing, deemed her a sympathizer of the insurgent group Barisan Revolusi Nasional (BRN), and falsely claimed that she was a supporter of the deadly militant ambush in Narathiwat province on July 22. Similar claims were shared about Anchana and Romadon. HRW stated that the abusive social media posts were part of a broader state-orchestrated initiative, with accounts being traced back to the Thai government’s information operations. Angkhana, a senator and former commissioner of the National Human Rights Commission of Thailand, has long been the subject of a state-sponsored campaign of intimidation for her frontline work in advocating for the rights of Thailand’s Muslim community. title: US announces economic sanctions against foreign entities accused of backing Iran
content: The US Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced economic sanctions against six “entities” (businesses and individuals) that it accuses of supporting Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). The companies are based in China, Russia, India and Iran. The IRGC is Iran’s military and one of the most powerful forces in the country. The new sanctions focus on two Iranian companies. Mahan Air is a privately-owned Iranian airline which OFAC accuses of being “the IRGC’s airline of choice for moving weapons, military personnel, and equipment,” including drones. DadeNegar Startup Studio is a tech company which OFAC accuses of being an IRGC front that has solicited the locations of American and Israeli equipment for the IRGC to target. DadeNegar did this by crowd-sourcing the information with a web site open to the public, obtaining the data for free. The sanctions are part of the US-Iran War , which is in its sixth month. OFAC says that China‑based Tang Xin, who is the managing director of Shanghai Wings Logistics Company, has coordinated travel for Mahan Air. Tang Xin is also the executive director and 50 percent owner of Shanghai Elite International Travel Company. OFAC says that Tang and Shanghai Wings have “assisted, sponsored, or provided financial, material, or technological support for, or goods or services to or in support of, Mahan Air,” by moving troops and weapons. India-based Skiez Travels and Logistics Private Limited and Russia-based Air Cargo Pro Limited have served as Mahan Air’s general sales agents in their respective countries. Shanghai Elite has been sanctioned for “being owned, controlled, or directed by, or having acted or purported to act for on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Tang Xin.” OFAC says that the sanctions are authorized under Executive Order 13224 , as amended.
